title: CHAPTER 12: NUTRITION, VITAMINS AND DEFICIENCY DISEASES

blocks.content: 1. Nutrition – Concept and Role in Life

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Carbohydrates serve as the primary and quickest energy source, stored as starch in plants and glycogen or fat in animals.
Proteins are built from amino acids and are vital for tissue growth, repair, and synthesis of enzymes, hormones, antibodies, and hemoglobin.
Fats yield twice the energy of carbohydrates, assist in fat-soluble vitamin absorption, and reserve energy in body tissue.
Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) accumulate in the liver and fat tissues, whereas water-soluble vitamins (B-complex, C) are not stored and require regular dietary intake.
Deficiencies in key minerals lead to conditions such as anemia (iron), goitre (iodine), osteoporosis (calcium), and dental issues (fluoride).

blocks.content:
Nutrition is the fundamental life process by which organisms take in food and utilize it for energy, growth, repair, and regulation of body processes.
All living organisms require nutrition to carry out metabolism.
Food provides raw materials for building tissues, repairing damaged cells, and producing energy.
Proper nutrition ensures normal physical growth, mental development, immunity, and longevity.
Poor nutrition leads to weakness, stunted growth, low immunity, and various deficiency diseases.
Nutrition involves a series of steps such as ingestion, digestion, absorption, assimilation, and egestion.
2. Types of Nutrition

Nutrition is broadly classified into autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition.
Autotrophic nutrition is found in green plants which prepare their own food by photosynthesis.
Heterotrophic nutrition is found in animals and non-green plants.
Heterotrophic nutrition includes holozoic, saprophytic, and parasitic nutrition.
Humans follow holozoic nutrition where food is ingested, digested, absorbed, and assimilated.
Understanding types of nutrition helps in understanding food habits of organisms.
3. Nutrients – Definition and Classification

Nutrients are chemical substances present in food that are required by the body.
They provide energy, build body tissues, and regulate metabolic activities.
Nutrients are classified into macronutrients and micronutrients.
Macronutrients include carbohydrates, proteins, and fats.
Micronutrients include vitamins and minerals.
Water and roughage are also essential components of diet.
4. Carbohydrates – Structure, Types and Functions

Carbohydrates are organic compounds made of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen.
They are the primary and quickest source of energy for the body.
Carbohydrates are of three types: monosaccharides, disaccharides, and polysaccharides.
Glucose is the most important monosaccharide.
Starch is the main storage carbohydrate in plants.
Excess carbohydrates are stored as glycogen or fat.
Deficiency leads to fatigue and ketosis.
5. Proteins – Importance and Biological Value

Proteins are complex organic compounds made of amino acids.
They are essential for growth, repair, and maintenance of tissues.
Proteins form enzymes, hormones, antibodies, and hemoglobin.
Proteins are classified as first-class (animal proteins) and second-class (plant proteins).
Protein deficiency causes diseases like kwashiorkor and marasmus.
Proteins cannot be stored and must be taken regularly.
6. Fats – Role and Metabolism
Vitamins do not provide energy but are essential for health.

Fats are concentrated sources of energy.
They provide twice the energy of carbohydrates.
Fats help in absorption of fat-soluble vitamins.
They protect organs and help maintain body temperature.
Fats are stored as reserve energy.
Deficiency causes dry skin and poor growth, while excess leads to obesity.
7. Vitamins – Definition and General Functions

Vitamins are organic compounds required in small quantities.
They regulate metabolism and prevent deficiency diseases.
Vitamins do not provide energy but are essential for health.
They act as coenzymes in biochemical reactions.
Vitamins are sensitive to heat, light, and air.
Balanced diet supplies sufficient vitamins.
8. Fat-Soluble Vitamins (A, D, E, K)

Fat-soluble vitamins are stored in liver and body fat.
Vitamin A is essential for vision and epithelial health.
Vitamin D regulates calcium and phosphorus metabolism.
Vitamin E protects cells from oxidative damage.
Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting.
Excess intake may cause toxicity.
9. Water-Soluble Vitamins (B-complex and C)

Water-soluble vitamins are not stored in body.
Vitamin B-complex includes B1, B2, B3, B6, and B12.
They are essential for metabolism and nervous system.
Vitamin C helps in wound healing and immunity.
Deficiency of water-soluble vitamins occurs easily.

blocks.content: 10. Vitamin Deficiency Diseases

Vitamin deficiencies lead to characteristic diseases.
Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness.
Vitamin D deficiency causes rickets and osteomalacia.
Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy.
Vitamin B1 deficiency causes beriberi.
Vitamin B12 deficiency causes pernicious anemia.
11. Minerals – Role and Classification

Minerals are inorganic nutrients required for normal body functions.
They are classified into macro-minerals and micro-minerals.
Calcium and phosphorus are required for bones and teeth.
Iron is required for hemoglobin.
Iodine is required for thyroid hormone.
Minerals regulate enzyme activities.
12. Mineral Deficiency Disorders

Iron deficiency leads to anemia.
Iodine deficiency causes goitre.
Calcium deficiency causes osteoporosis.
Fluoride deficiency leads to dental problems.
Mineral imbalance affects metabolism and growth.
13. Water and Roughage

Water is essential for all metabolic reactions.
It helps in digestion, absorption, and excretion.
Roughage adds bulk to food and prevents constipation.
It improves intestinal movement.
Adequate water intake is essential for health.

items: Vitamin B1 deficiency causes beriberi, whereas Vitamin B12 deficiency results in pernicious anemia.
Vitamin C deficiency leads to scurvy, and Vitamin D deficiency causes rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.
Iron deficiency causes anemia, while iodine deficiency leads to goitre through thyroid dysfunction.
Proteins are body-building nutrients that cannot be stored in the human body and must be consumed regularly.

blocks.content: 14. Balanced Diet – Concept and Importance

Balanced diet contains all nutrients in appropriate proportions.
It depends on age, sex, occupation, and climate.
Balanced diet prevents malnutrition.
It maintains ideal body weight.
It improves immunity and work efficiency.
15. Malnutrition – Types and Effects

Malnutrition is caused by inadequate or excess nutrition.
Undernutrition leads to deficiency diseases.
Overnutrition leads to obesity and lifestyle diseases.
Children and pregnant women are highly affected.
Malnutrition affects physical and mental development.
16. IMPORTANT FACTS – SSC FOCUS

• Nutrition is essential for life.
• Carbohydrates are main energy source.
• Proteins are body-building nutrients.
• Fats provide maximum energy.
• Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness.
• Vitamin D deficiency causes rickets.
• Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy.
• Iron deficiency causes anemia.
• Iodine deficiency causes goitre.
• Balanced diet maintains health.
